entries.1e78f138d3a768ba5111459ee80bd2b5f7ae535b: <div sID="gen9045" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Esth.6" sID="Esth.6"/> <div eID="gen9045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9046" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9047" type="x-p"/> It is a very surprising scene that opens in this chapter. Haman, when he hoped to be Mordecai's judge, was made his page, to his great confusion and mortification; and thus way was made for the defeat of Haman's plot and the deliverance of the Jews. I. The providence of God recommends Mordecai in the night to the king's favour, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1-Esth.6.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Haman, who came to incense the king against him, is employed as an instrument of the king's favour to him, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.4-Esth.6.11">ver. 4-11</reference>. III. From this his friends read him his doom, which is executed in the next chapter, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.12-Esth.6.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. And now it appears that Esther's intercession for her people was happily adjourned, <hi type="italic">De die in diem—from day to day.</hi>
entries.f423ef34d52251d7844fe84daed0c0043a91ecd0: <div eID="gen9047" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9046" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Record of Mordecai's Loyalty. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him. <div eID="gen9048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9049" type="x-p"/> Now Satan put it into the heart of Haman to contrive Mordecai's death we read in the foregoing chapter; how God put it into the heart of the king to contrive Mordecai's honour we are here told. Now, if the king's word will prevail above Haman's (for, though Haman be a great man, the king in the throne must be above him), much more will the <hi type="italic">counsel of God stand,</hi> whatever <hi type="italic">devices there are in men's hearts.</hi> It is to no purpose therefore for Haman to oppose it, when both God and the king will have Mordecai honoured, and in this juncture too, when his preferment, and Haman's disappointment, would help to ripen the great affair of the Jewish deliverance for the effort that Esther was to make towards it the next day. Sometimes delay may prove to have been good conduct. Stay awhile, and we may have done the sooner. <hi type="italic">Cunctando restituit rem—He conquered by delay.</hi> Let us trace the steps which Providence took towards the advancement of Mordecai. <div eID="gen9049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9050" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">On that night could not the king sleep.</hi> His <hi type="italic">sleep fled away</hi> (so the word is); and perhaps, like a shadow, the more carefully he pursued it the further it went from him. Sometimes we cannot sleep because we fain would sleep. Even after a banquet of wine he could not sleep when Providence had a design to serve in keeping him waking. We read of no bodily indisposition he was under, that might break his sleep; but God, <hi type="italic">whose gift sleep is,</hi> withheld it from him. Those that are ever so much resolved to cast away care cannot always do it; they find it in their pillows when they neither expect nor welcome it. He that commanded 127 provinces could not command one hour's sleep. Perhaps the charms of Esther's conversation the day before gave occasion to his heart to reproach him for neglecting her, and banishing her from his presence, though she was the wife of his bosom, for above thirty days; and that might keep him waking. An offended conscience can find a time to speak when it will be heard. <div eID="gen9050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9051" type="x-p"/> II. When he could not sleep he called to have the book of records, the Journals of his reign, read to him, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1">v. 1</reference>. Surely he did not design that that should lull him asleep; it would rather fill his head with cares, and drive away sleep. But God put it into his heart to call for it, rather than for music or songs, which the Persian kings used to be attended with (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.18">Dan. vi. 18</reference>) and which would have been more likely to compose him to rest. When men do that which is unaccountable we know not what God intends by it. Perhaps he would have this book of business read to him that he might improve time and be forming some useful projects. Had it been king David's case, he would have found some other entertainment for his thoughts; when he could not sleep he would have remembered God and meditated upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Ps. lxiv. 6</reference>), and, if he would have had any book read to him, it would have been his Bible; for <hi type="italic">in that law did he meditate day and night.</hi> <div eID="gen9051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9052" type="x-p"/> III. The servant that read to him either lighted first on that article which concerned Mordecai, or, reading long, came to it at length. Among other things it was found written that Mordecai had discovered a plot against the life of the king which prevented the execution of it, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.2">v. 2</reference>. Mordecai was not in such favour at court that the reader should designedly pitch upon that place; but Providence directed him to it; nay, if we may believe the Jews' tradition (as bishop Patrick relates it), opening the book at this place he turned over the leaves, and would have read another part of the book, but the leaves flew back again to the same place where he opened it; so that he was forced to read that paragraph. How Mordecai's good service was recorded we read <reference osisRef="Esth.2.23">ch. ii. 23</reference>, and here it is found upon record. <div eID="gen9052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9053" type="x-p"/> IV. The king enquired <hi type="italic">what honour and dignity had been done to Mordecai</hi> for this, suspecting that this good service had gone unrewarded, and, like Pharaoh's butler, remembering it as <hi type="italic">his fault this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.41.9">Gen. xli. 9</reference>. Note, The law of gratitude is a law of nature. We ought particularly to be grateful to our inferiors, and not to think all their services such debts to us but that they make us indebted to them. Two rules of gratitude may be gathered from the king's enquiry here:—1. Better honour than nothing. If we cannot, or need not, make recompence to those who have been kind to us, yet let us do them honour by acknowledging their kindnesses and owning our obligations to them. 2. Better late than never. If we have long neglected to make grateful returns for good offices done us, let us at length bethink ourselves of our debts. <div eID="gen9053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9054" type="x-p"/> V. The servants informed him that nothing had been done to Mordecai for that eminent service; in the king's gate he sat before, and there he still sat. Note, 1. It is common for great men to take little notice of their inferiors. The king knew not whether Mordecai was preferred or no till his servants informed him. High spirits take a pride in being careless and unconcerned about those that are below them and ignorant of their state. The great God takes cognizance of the meanest of his servants, knows what dignity is done them and what disgrace. 2. Humility, modesty, and self-denial, though in God's account of great price, yet commonly hinder men's preferment in the world. Mordecai rises no higher than the king's gate, while proud ambitious Haman gets the king's ear and heart; but, though the aspiring rise fast, the humble stand fast. Honour makes proud men giddy, but <hi type="italic">upholds the humble in spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.23">Prov. xxix. 23</reference>. 3. Honour and dignity are rated high in the king's books. He does not ask, What reward has been given Mordecai? what money? what estate? but only, What honour?—a poor thing, and which, if he had not wherewith to support it, would be but a burden. 4. The greatest merits and the best services are often overlooked and go unrewarded among men. Little honour is done to those who best deserve it, and fittest for it, and would do most good with it. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.14-Eccl.9.16">Eccl. ix. 14-16</reference>. The acquisition of wealth and honour is usually a perfect lottery, in which those that venture least commonly carry off the best prize. Nay, 5. Good services are sometimes so far from being a man's preferment that they will not be his protection. Mordecai is at this time, by the king's edict, doomed to destruction, with all the Jews, though it is owned that he deserved dignity. Those that faithfully serve God need not fear being thus ill paid.
entries.812b690de85987e0157efbca428e74e9aa3e04fb: <div eID="gen9054" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Honour Conferred on Mordecai. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9055" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And the king said, Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the court? Now Haman was come into the outward court of the king's house, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the king's servants said unto him, Behold, Haman standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in. <hi type="super">6</hi> So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself? <hi type="super">7</hi> And Haman answered the king, For the man whom the king delighteth to honour, <hi type="super">8</hi> Let the royal apparel be brought which the king <hi type="italic">useth</hi> to wear, and the horse that the king rideth upon, and the crown royal which is set upon his head: <hi type="super">9</hi> And let this apparel and horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king's most noble princes, that they may array the man <hi type="italic">withal</hi> whom the king delighteth to honour, and bring him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaim before him, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then the king said to Haman, Make haste, <hi type="italic">and</hi> take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king's gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour. <div eID="gen9055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9056" type="x-p"/> It is now morning, and people begin to stir. <div eID="gen9056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9057" type="x-p"/> I. Haman is so impatient to get Mordecai hanged that he comes early to court, to be ready at the king's levee, before any other business is brought before him, to get a warrant for his execution (<reference osisRef="Esth.6.4">v. 4</reference>), which he makes sure that he shall have at the first word. The king would gratify him in a greater thing than that; and he could tell the king that he was so confident of the justice of his request, and the king's favour to him in it, that he had got the gallows ready: one word from the king would complete his satisfaction. <div eID="gen9057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9058" type="x-p"/> II. The king is so impatient to have Mordecai honoured that he sends to know who is in the court that is fit to be employed in it. Word is brought him that Haman is in the court, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.5">v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let him come in,</hi> says the king, the fittest man to be made use of both in directing and in dispensing the king's favour; and the king knew nothing of any quarrel he had with Mordecai. Haman is brought in immediately, proud of the honour done him in being admitted into the king's bed-chamber, as it should seem, <hi type="italic">before he was up;</hi> for let the king but give orders for the dignifying of Mordecai, and he will be easy in his mind and try to sleep. Now Haman thinks he has the fairest opportunity he can wish for to solicit against Mordecai; but the king's heart is as full as his, and it is fit he should speak first. <div eID="gen9058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9059" type="x-p"/> III. The king asks Haman how he should express his favour to one whom he had marked for a favourite: <hi type="italic">What shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honour?</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.6.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, It is a good property in kings, and other superiors, to delight in bestowing rewards and not to delight in punishing. Parents and masters should take a pleasure in commending and encouraging that which is good in those under their charge. <div eID="gen9059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9060" type="x-p"/> IV. Haman concludes that he himself is the favourite intended, and therefore prescribes the highest expressions of honour that could, for once, be bestowed upon a subject. His proud heart presently suggested, "To whom will the king delight to do honour more than to myself? No one deserves it so well as I," thinks Haman, "nor stands so fair for it." See how men's pride deceives them. 1. Haman had a better opinion of his merits than there was cause for: he thought none so worthy of honour as himself. It is a foolish thing for us thus to think ourselves the only deserving persons, or more deserving than any other. The deceitfulness of our own hearts appears in nothing so much as in the good conceit we have of ourselves and our own performances, against which we should therefore constantly watch and pray. 2. He had a better opinion of his interest than there was reason for. He thought the king loved and valued no one but himself, but he was deceived. We should suspect that the esteem which others profess for us is not so great as it seems to be or as we are sometimes willing to believe it is, that we may not think too well of ourselves nor place too much confidence in others. Now Haman thinks he is carving out honour for himself, and therefore does it very liberally, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.8-Esth.6.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. Nay, he does it presumptuously, prescribing honours too great to be conferred upon any subject, that he must be dressed in the royal robes, wear the royal crown, and ride on the king's own horse; in short, he must appear in all the pomp and grandeur of the king himself, only he must not carry the sceptre, the emblem of power. He must be attended by one of <hi type="italic">the king's most noble princes,</hi> who must be his lacquey, and all the people must be made to take notice of him and do him reverence; for he must ride in state through the streets, and it must be <hi type="italic">proclaimed before him,</hi> for his honour, and the encouragement of all to seek the ruler's favour, <hi type="italic">Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honour,</hi> which had the same intention with that which was proclaimed before Joseph, <hi type="italic">Bow the knee;</hi> for every good subject will honour those whom the king delights to honour. And shall not every good Christian then honour those whom the King of kings delights to honour and call the <hi type="italic">saints that are on the earth the excellent ones?</hi> <div eID="gen9060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9061" type="x-p"/> V. The king confounds him with a positive order that he should immediately go himself and put all this honour upon Mordecai the Jew, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.10">v. 10</reference>. If the king had but said, as Haman expected, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man,</hi> what a fair opportunity would he have had to do the errand he came on, and to desire that, to grace the solemnity of his triumphs, Mordecai, his sworn enemy, might be hanged at the same time! But how is he thunderstruck when the king bids him not to order all this to be done, but to do it himself to Mordecai the Jew, the very man he hated above all men and whose ruin he was now designing! Now, it is to no purpose to think of moving any thing to the king against Mordecai when he is <hi type="italic">the man whom the king delights to honour.</hi> Solomon says, <hi type="italic">The heart of the king is unsearchable</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Prov. xxv. 3</reference>), but it is not unchangeable. <div eID="gen9061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9062" type="x-p"/> VI. Haman dares not dispute nor so much as seem to dislike the king's order, but, with the greatest regret and reluctance imaginable, brings it to Mordecai, who I suppose did no more cringe to Haman now than he had done, valuing his counterfeit respect no more than he had valued his concealed malice. The apparel is brought, Mordecai is dressed up, and rides in state through the city, recognized as the king's favourite, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.11">v. 11</reference>. It is hard to say which of the two put a greater force upon himself, proud Haman in putting this honour upon Mordecai, or humble Mordecai in accepting it: the king would have it so, and both must submit. Upon <hi type="italic">this</hi> account it was agreeable to Mordecai as it was an indication of the king's favour, and gave hope that Esther would prevail for the reversing of the edict against the Jews.
entries.0930b30fcd382d9b928212067190a11a0fa782c5: <div eID="gen9062" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Haman Cast Down. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9063" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every <hi type="italic">thing</hi> that had befallen him. Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai <hi type="italic">be</hi> of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And while they <hi type="italic">were</hi> yet talking with him, came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared. <div eID="gen9063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9064" type="x-p"/> We may here observe, <div eID="gen9064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9065" type="x-p"/> I. How little Mordecai was puffed up with his advancement. He <hi type="italic">came again to the king's gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.6.12">v. 12</reference>); he returned to his place and the duty of it immediately, and minded his business as closely as he had done before. Honour is well bestowed on those that are not made proud and idle by it, and will not think themselves above their business. <div eID="gen9065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9066" type="x-p"/> II. How much Haman was cast down with his disappointment. He could not bear it. To wait upon any man, especially Mordecai, and at this time, when he hoped to have seen him hanged, was enough to break such a proud heart as he had. He <hi type="italic">hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered,</hi> as one that looked upon himself as sunk and in a manner condemned. What harm had it done him to stoop thus to Mordecai? Was he ever the worse for it? Was it not what he himself proposed to be done by <hi type="italic">one of the king's most noble princes?</hi> Why then should he grudge to do it himself? But that will break a proud man's heart which would not break a humble man's sleep. <div eID="gen9066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9067" type="x-p"/> III. How his doom was, out of this event, read to him by his wife and his friends: "If Mordecai be, as they say he is, <hi type="italic">of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall,</hi> though but in a point of honour, never expect to <hi type="italic">prevail against him;</hi> for thou <hi type="italic">shalt surely fall before him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Esth.6.13">v. 13</reference>. Miserable comforters were they all; they did not advise him to repent, and ask Mordecai's pardon for his bad design against him, but foretold his destiny as fatal and unavoidable. Two things they foresaw:—1. That Haman would be disappointed in his enterprise against the Jews: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not prevail</hi> to root out that people. Heaven plainly fights against thee." 2. That he himself would be destroyed: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt surely fall before him.</hi> The contest between Michael and the dragon will not be a drawn battle; no, Haman must fall before Mordecai. Two things they grounded their prognostications upon:—(1.) This Mordecai was <hi type="italic">of the seed of the Jews; feeble Jews</hi> their enemies sometimes called them, but formidable Jews they sometimes found them. They are a holy seed, a praying seed, in covenant with God, and a seed that the Lord hath all along blessed, and therefore let not their enemies expect to triumph over them. (2.) Haman had begun to fall, and therefore he was certainly a gone man. It has been observed of great court-favourites that when once they have been frowned upon they have fallen utterly, as fast as they rose; it is true of the church's enemies that when God begins with them he will make an end. As for God his work is perfect. <div eID="gen9067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9068" type="x-p"/> IV. How seasonably he was now sent for to the banquet that Esther had prepared, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.14">v. 14</reference>. He thought it seasonable, in hopes it would revive his drooping spirits and save his sinking honour. But really it was seasonable because, his spirits being broken by this sore disappointment, he might the more easily be run down by Esther's complaint against him. The wisdom of God is seen in timing the means of his church's deliverance so as to manifest his own glory.  <chapter eID="Esth.6"/> <div eID="gen9068" type="x-p"/>

entries.c815b462b450f00f3d6bc622c1b06bfa0d4ec8d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4429"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.6.1-Esth.6.14">Es 6:1-14</reference>. Ahasuerus Rewards Mordecai for Former Service.</title> <div sID="gen6406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4429"/><hi type="bold">1. the king ... commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles--</hi>In Eastern courts, there are scribes or officers whose duty it is to keep a journal of every occurrence worthy of notice. A book of this kind, abounding with anecdotes, is full of interest. It has been a custom with Eastern kings, in all ages, frequently to cause the annals of the kingdom to be read to them. It is resorted to, not merely as a pastime to while away the tedium of an hour, but as a source of instruction to the monarch, by reviewing the important incidents of his own life, as well as those of his ancestors. There was, therefore, nothing uncommon in this Persian monarch calling for the court journal. But, in his being unable to sleep at that particular juncture, in his ordering the book then to be read to him, and in his attention having been specially directed to the important and as yet unrewarded services of Mordecai, the immediate interposition of Providence is distinctly visible. <div eID="gen6406" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b2701ae67f2390a9cade2675d27a4490d7729af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4430"/><div sID="gen6407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4430"/><hi type="bold">4. Now Haman was come into the outward court--</hi>This was early in the morning. It is the invariable custom for kings in Eastern countries to transact business before the sun is hot, often in the open air, and so Haman was in all probability come officially to attend on his master. <div eID="gen6407" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cf2a24253715335d58260a5f836a2ccad6aa5d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4431"/><div sID="gen6408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4431"/><hi type="bold">6. What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour?--</hi>In bestowing tokens of their favor, the kings of Persia do not at once, and as it were by their own will, determine the kind of honor that shall be awarded; but they turn to the courtier standing next in rank to themselves, and ask him what shall be done to the individual who has rendered the service specified; and according to the answer received, the royal mandate is issued. <div eID="gen6408" type="x-p"/>
entries.d662aa7a07be37c73cca4d0ec1dcb9b3565ec8e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4432"/><div sID="gen6409" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4432"/><hi type="bold">8. the royal apparel ... which the king useth to wear--</hi>A coat which has been on the back of a king or prince is reckoned a most honorable gift, and is given with great ceremony.<div eID="gen6409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the horse that the king rideth upon--</hi>Persia was a country of horses, and the highbred charger that the king rode upon acquired, in the eyes of his venal subjects, a sort of sacredness from that circumstance.<div eID="gen6410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the crown royal which is set upon his head--</hi>either the royal turban, or it may be a tiara, with which, on state processions, the horse's head was adorned. <div eID="gen6411" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf38cd079eefaf53b33dd2e455df42427cbf75c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4433"/><div sID="gen6412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4433"/><hi type="bold">9. delivered to the hand of one of the king's most noble princes ... array the man--</hi>On grand and public occasions, the royal steed is led by the highest subject through the principal streets of the city, a ceremony which may occupy several hours. <div eID="gen6412" type="x-p"/>
entries.c23db7cf5a0fda738fd97719b00bcfa92ae7fd37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4434"/><div sID="gen6413" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4434"/><hi type="bold">11. Then Haman took, &c.--</hi>This sudden reverse, however painful to Haman as an individual, is particularly characteristic of the Persian manners. <div eID="gen6413" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca068a39ec583f46398b0e8b74710aee90397d3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4435"/><div sID="gen6414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4435"/><hi type="bold">14. came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared--</hi>Besides the invitation given to an entertainment, a message is always sent to the guests, immediately at the day and hour appointed, to announce that all things are ready. <chapter eID="Esth.6"/>

entries.fda05a1238969357e004df6b48bce85d747c52bd: <div eID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15558" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15558" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> That night the king, not being able to sleep, orders the chronicles of the kingdom to be read to him; and finds there the record concerning the discovery of the treason of the two eunuchs, made by Mordecai, <reference osisRef="Est.6.1">Est 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.6.2">Est 6:2</reference>. He inquires whether Mordecai had been rewarded, and was answered in the negative, <reference osisRef="Est.6.3">Est 6:3</reference>. At this time Haman arrives, in order to request the king's permission to hang Mordecai; and being suddenly asked what should be done to the man whom the king delighted to honor, supposing that himself must be meant, presented the ceremonial, <reference osisRef="Est.6.4-Est.6.9">Est 6:4-9</reference>. The king orders him to give Mordecai those honors; which he performs, to his extreme mortification, <reference osisRef="Est.6.10">Est 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.6.11">Est 6:11</reference>. He informs his wife Zeresh of these transactions, who predicts his downfall, <reference osisRef="Est.6.12-Est.6.13">Est 6:12-13</reference>. He is hurried by the eunuchs to the queen's banquet, <reference osisRef="Est.6.14">Est 6:14</reference>. <div eID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> On that night could not the king sleep - The Targum says the king had a dream, which was as follows: - "And the king saw one in the similitude of a man who spoke these words to him: Haman desireth to slay thee, and to make himself king in thy stead. Behold, he will come unto thee early in the morning, to ask from thee the man who rescued thee from death, that he may slay him: but say thou unto Haman, What shall be done for the man whose honor the king studieth? And thou wilt find that he will ask nothing less from thee than the royal vestments, the regal crown, and the horse on which the king is wont to ride." <div eID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> The records of the chronicles - It may be well asked, Why should the king, in such a perturbed state of mind, wish such a dry detail, as chronicles afford, to be read to him? But the truth is, as chronicles were composed among the Persians, he could not have brought before him any work more instructive, and more entertaining; because they were all written in verse, and were generally the work of the most eminent poets in the empire. They are written in this way to the present time; and the famous epic poem of the finest Persian poet, Ferdusi, the Homer of India, is nothing else than a collection of chronicles brought down from the creation to the reign of Mohammed Ghezny, in the beginning of the tenth century. After thirty years' labor, he finished this poem, which contained one hundred and twenty thousand lines, and presented it to the Sultan Mahmoud, who had promised to give him a dinar (eight shillings and sixpence) for every line. The poem was finished a.d. 984; and was formed out of compositions of a similar nature made by former poets. This chronological poem is written in all the harmony, strength, and elegance of the most beautiful and harmonious language in the universe; and what adds greatly to its worth is, that it has few Arabic words, with which the beautiful Persian tongue was loaded, and in my opinion corrupted, after the conquest of the major part of Asia by the Mohammedans. The pedants of Hindoostan, whether they speak or write, in prose or in verse, affect this commixture of Arabic words; which, though they subjugate them to Persian rules, are producing a ruggedness in a language, which in Ferdusi, flows deep and strong like a river of oil over every kind of channel. Such, I suppose, was the chronicle that was read to Ahasuerus, when his distractions prevented his sleep, and his troubled mind required that soothing repose which the gentle though powerful hand of poetry is alone, in such circumstances, capable of affording. Even our rough English ancestors had their poetic chronicles; and, among many, the chronicle of Robert of Gloucester is proof in point. I need not add, that all that is real in Ossian is of the same complexion.
entries.4b513afe725742c52c98583e010d08bd9541b295: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> What honor and dignity hath been done to Mordecai - It is certain he found nothing in the record; and had any thing been done, that was the most likely place to find it.
entries.e9a3d4b5cb40c50488b3490bab23ccb0cf97990a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> Who is in the court? - This accords with the dream mentioned by the Targum; and given above. <div eID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15566" type="x-p"/> Now Haman was come - This must have been very early in the morning. Haman's pride and revenge were both on the tenters to be gratified.
entries.fdba1d8e8b992007ff830b7497d384c7b5a0af51: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15567" type="x-p"/> The king said unto him - He did not give him time to make his request; and put a question to him which, at the first view, promised him all that his heart could wish.
entries.616d0b2f115877e96f13c75881707c046694b097: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15568" type="x-p"/> Let the royal apparel be brought - Pride and folly ever go hand in hand. What he asked would have been in any ordinary case against his own life: but he wished to reach the pinnacle of honor: never reflecting that the higher he rose, the more terrible would be his fall. The royal apparel was never worn but by the king: even when the king had lain them aside, it was death to put them on. The Targum has purple robes. <div eID="gen15568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15569" type="x-p"/> And the horse - and the crown royal - Interpreters are greatly divided whether what is called here the crown royal be not rather an ornament worn on the head of the horse, than what may be called the royal crown. The original may be understood both ways; and our version seems to favor the former opinion; but I think it more likely that the royal crown is meant; for why mention the ordinary trappings of the royal steed?
entries.32d1615d29951827623acd85c3c17a258bcd2bb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15570" type="x-p"/> One of the king's most noble princes - Alas, Poor Haman! Never was the fable of the dog and shadow more literally fulfilled. Thou didst gape at the shadow, and didst lose the substance.
entries.f38716509ccb8796abe5310cca5b370b3c24b247: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15571" type="x-p"/> Make haste, and take the apparel - and do even so to Mordecai - O mortifying reverse of human fortune! How could Haman bear this? The Targumist might speak according to nature when he said that "Haman besought the king to kill him rather than degrade him so." How astonishing is the conduct of Divine providence in all this business! From it we plainly see that there is neither counsel nor wisdom against the Lord; and that he who digs a pit for his neighbor, is sure to fall into it himself.
entries.df0ec9397a5b6b4bb5db77c93074ca0d97bb35f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen15571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15572" type="x-p"/> Mordecai came again to the king's gate - He resumed his former humble state; while Haman, ashamed to look up, covered his face, and ran home to hide himself in his own house. Covering the head and face was a sign of shame and confusion, as well as of grief, among most people of the earth.
entries.7802298da824b61ede87dd3511593e909ea0b00b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15573" type="x-p"/> But shalt surely fall before him - The Septuagint adds, ὁτι ὁ Θεος ὁ ζων μετ' αυτου, for the living God is with him. But this is a sentiment that could scarcely be expected to proceed from the mouth of heathens, such as these were.
entries.4716b156d01442fdfc03bbc505482f7d7d840137: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15574" type="x-p"/> Hasted to bring Haman - There was a dreadful banquet before him, of which he knew nothing: and he could have little appetite to enjoy that which he knew was prepared at the palace of Esther. <div eID="gen15574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15575" type="x-p"/> One grand design of this history is, to show that he who lays a snare for the life of his neighbor, is most likely to fall into it himself: for, in the course of the Divine providence, men generally meet with those evils in life which they have been the means of inflicting on others: and this is exactly agreeable to the saying of our Lord: "With what measure ye mete it shall be measured to you withal."  <chapter eID="Esth.6"/> <div eID="gen15575" type="x-p"/>

entries.e90adc11a6ea1fe21481bb92ee50ca136b812b9b: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1">Est 6:1</reference> <div eID="gen6764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6765" type="x-p"/> An unexpected turn of affairs. Est 6:1. On that night between Esther’s first and second banquet, the king’s sleep fled, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles and to read therefrom. On הזּכרנות ספר, comp. Ezr 4:15. The title is here more particularly stated than in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.23">Est 2:23</reference>, where the book is briefly called: The book of the chronicles. נקראים ויּהיוּ, and they (the chronicles) were read before the king. The participle denotes the long continuance of this reading.
entries.d29c0a82eff7af3dd05d40ecfebe7e9a9e714ddb: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.2">Est 6:2</reference> <div eID="gen6765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6766" type="x-p"/> And it was found written therein among other matters, that Mordochai had given information concerning the two courtiers who were plotting against the king’s life. This is the conspiracy related <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Est 2:21</reference>-23. The name Bigthana is in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Est 2:21</reference> written Bigthan.
entries.cf42d790e51ad4bfcc8f1cb892cd08e69370c8d7: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.3">Est 6:3</reference> <div eID="gen6766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6767" type="x-p"/> On this occasion the king asked: What honour and greatness hath been done to Mordochai for this? על־זה, for giving this information. And the king’s servants answered: Nothing has been shown him. עם עשׂה, to show any one something, e.g., favour; comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.6">2Sa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.8">2Sa 3:8</reference>, and elsewhere. גּדוּלה, greatness, i.e., promotion to honour.
entries.447dbb0febce7005c3fbbaf3183ee4b4c24a0811: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.4">Est 6:4</reference> <div eID="gen6767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6768" type="x-p"/> To repair this deficiency, and to do honour to the man who had done good service to the king - as the Persian monarchs were accustomed, comp. Brisson, <hi type="italic">de reg. Pers. princ.</hi> i. c. 135 - he asked, “who is in the court?” i.e., whether some minister or state functionary were there with whom he might consult concerning the honour due to Mordochai. Those who desired an audience with the king were accustomed to appear and wait in the outer court, until they were summoned into the inner court to present themselves before the monarch. From this question of the king it appears that it was already morning. And Haman, it is parenthetically remarked, was come into the outer court to speak to the king, to hang Mordochai on the tree which he had prepared.
entries.1abe6f42995f6ead12074317bf494dff95816f81: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.5">Est 6:5</reference> <div eID="gen6768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6769" type="x-p"/> The attendants inform the king that Haman is in the court; whereupon the king commands: יבוא, let him come in.
entries.c31dd8f90306df43588090339140f465d05fb8c7: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.6-Esth.6.9">Est 6:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen6769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6770" type="x-p"/> As soon as he enters the king asks: What is to be done to the man in whose honour the king delighteth? i.e., whom he delights to honour. And Haman, thinking (בּלבּו אמר, to say in one’s heart, i.e., to think) to whom will the king delight to show honour more than to me (ממּבּי יותר, projecting before me, surpassing me, hence adverbially, beyond me, e.g., <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.12">Ecc 12:12</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.15">Ecc 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ecc 7:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ecc 7:16</reference>)? votes immediately for the greatest possible mark of honour, and says, Est 6:7.: “As for the man in whose honour the king delighteth, let them bring the royal apparel with which the king has been clothed, and a horse on which the king has ridden, and the king’s crown upon his head, and let them deliver this apparel and horse to one of the chief princes of the king, and let them array (i.e., with the royal apparel) the man in whose honour the king delighteth, and cause him to ride upon the horse through the streets of the city, and proclaim before him: Thus shall it be done to the man in whose honour the king delighteth.” וגו אשׁר אישׁ, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.7">Est 6:7</reference>, precedes absolutely, and the predicate does not follow till והלבּישׁוּ, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.9">Est 6:9</reference>, where the preceding subject is now by an anacoluthon taken up in the accusative (את־האישׁ). Several clauses are inserted between, for the purpose of enumerating beforehand all that appertains to such a token of honour: a royal garment, a royal steed, a crown on the head, and one of the chief princes for the carrying out of the honour awarded. The royal garment is not only, as Bertheau justly remarks, such a one as the king is accustomed to wear, but, as is shown by the perf. לבשׁ, one which the king has himself already put on or worn. Hence it is not an ordinary state-robe, the so-called Median apparel which the king himself, the chief princes among the Persians, and those on whom the king bestowed such raiment were wont to appear in (Herod. 3.84, 7.116; Xenoph. <hi type="italic">Cyrop</hi>. 8.3.1, comp. with the note of Baehr on Her. 3.84), but a costly garment, the property of the sovereign himself. This was the highest mark of honour that could be shown to a subject. So too was the riding upon a horse on which the king had ridden, and whose head was adorned with a royal crown. נתּן is perf. Niph., not 1st pers. pl. imperf. Kal, as Maurer insists; and בּראשׁו אשׁר refers to the head of the horse, not to the head of the man to be honoured, as Clericus, Rambach, and most ancient expositors explain the words, in opposition to the natural sense of - בּראשׁו נתּן אשׁר. We do not indeed find among classical writers any testimony to such an adornment of the royal steed; but the circumstance is not at all improbable, and seems to be corroborated by ancient remains, certain Assyrian and ancient Persian sculptures, representing the horses of the king, and apparently those of princes, with ornaments on their heads terminating in three points, which may be regarded as a kind of crown. The <hi type="italic">infin. absol.</hi> ונתון is a continuation of the preceding jussive יביאוּ: and they shall give, let them give the garment - to the hand of a man, i.e., hand or deliver to him. The garment and horse are to be delivered to one of the noblest princes, that he may bring them to the individual to be honoured, may array him in the garment, set him on the horse, and proclaim before him as he rides through the city, etc. On הפּרתּמים, comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.1.4">Est 1:4</reference>, and on the matter itself, Gen 41:43. רחוב is either an open square, the place of public assemblage, the forum, or a collective signifying the wide streets of the city. יעשׂה כּכה as in <reference osisRef="Deut.25.9">Deu 25:9</reference> and elsewhere.
entries.0a6a29777c8d5ba8bafb8a7d56fe71a596bcd74c: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.10-Esth.6.11">Est 6:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen6770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6771" type="x-p"/> This honour, then, the haughty Haman was now compelled to pay to the hated Jew. The king commanded him: “Make haste, take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said,” i.e., in the manner proposed by thee, “and do even so to Mordochai the Jew, that sitteth at the king’s gate; let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken,” i.e., carry out your proposal exactly. How the king knew that Mordochai was a Jew, and that he sat in the king’s gate, is not indeed expressly stated, but may easily be supplied from the conversation of the king with his servants concerning Mordochai’s discovery of the conspiracy, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1">Est 6:1</reference>-3. On this occasion the servants of the king would certainly give him particulars concerning Mordochai, who by daily frequenting the king’s gate, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Est 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">Est 5:9</reference>, would certainly have attracted the attention of all the king’s suite. Nor can doubt be case upon the historical truth of the fact related in this verse by the question: whether the king had forgotten that all Jews were doomed to destruction, and that he had delivered them up to Haman for that purpose (J. D. Mich.). Such forgetfulness in the case of such a monarch as Xerxes cannot surprise us.
entries.651173b1c9d153d744a5352a04b6e4d5c928572f: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.12-Esth.6.13">Est 6:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen6771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6772" type="x-p"/> After this honour had been paid him, Mordochai returned to the king’s gate; but Haman hasted to his house, “sad and with his head covered,” to relate to his wife and friends all that had befallen him. A deeper mortification he could not have experienced than that of being obliged, by the king’s command, publicly to show the highest honour to the very individual whose execution he was just about to propose to him. The covering of the head is a token of deep confusion and mourning; comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">Jer 14:4</reference>; 2Sa 15:30. Then his wise men, and Zeresh his wife, said to him: ”If Mordochai, before whom thou hast begun to fall, be of the seed of the Jews, thou wilt not prevail against him, but wholly fall before him.” לו תוּכל לא, <hi type="italic">non praevalebis ei,</hi> comp. Gen 32:26. תּפּול נפול with an emphatic <hi type="italic">infin. absol.:</hi> wholly fall. Instead of the חכמיו אהביו are here named, or to speak more correctly the friends of Haman are here called his wise men (magi). Even in <reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Est 5:14</reference> Haman’s friends figure as those with whom he takes counsel concerning Mordochai, i.e., as his counsellors or advisers; hence it is very probable that there were magi among their number, who now “come forward as a <hi type="italic">genus sapientum et doctorum</hi> (Cicero, <hi type="italic">divin</hi>. i. 23)” (Berth.), and predict his overthrow in his contest with Mordochai. The ground of this prediction is stated: “If Mordochai is of the seed of the Jews,” i.e., of Jewish descent, then after this preliminary fall a total fall is inevitable. Previously (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Est 5:14</reference>) they had not hesitated to advise him to hang the insignificant Jew; but now that the insignificant Jew has become, as by a miracle, a man highly honoured by the king, the fact that the Jews are under the special protection of Providence is pressed upon them. <hi type="italic">Ex fato populorum, remarks Grotius, de singulorum fatis judicabant. Judaei gravissime oppressi a Cyri temporibus contra spem omnem resurgere caeperant.</hi> We cannot, however, regard as well founded the further remark: <hi type="italic">de Amalecitis audierant oraculum esse, eos Judaeorum manu perituros,</hi> which Grotius, with most older expositors, derives from the Amalekite origin of Haman. The revival of the Jewish people since the times of Cyrus was sufficient to induce, in the minds of heathen who were attentive to the signs of the times, the persuasion that this nation enjoyed divine protection.
entries.23f4194ea023c1c9db8e2f89588b8a8b66889adb: <reference osisRef="Esth.6.14">Est 6:14</reference> <div eID="gen6772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6773" type="x-p"/> During this conversation certain courtiers had already arrived, who hastily brought Haman to the banquet of the queen, to which he would certainly go in a less happy state of mind than on the preceding day. Haman’s Downfall and Ruin - <reference osisRef="Esth.7.1-Esth.7.10">Est 7:1-10</reference> <div eID="gen6773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6774" type="x-p"/> At this second banquet the king again inquired of the queen what was her petition, when she entreated that her life and that of her people might be spared, for that she and her people were sold to destruction (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.1-Esth.7.4">Est 7:1-4</reference>). The king, evidently shocked at such a petition, asked who was the originator of so evil a deed, and Esther named the wicked Haman as the enemy (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.5">Est 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.6">Est 7:6</reference>). Full of indignation at such a crime, the king rose from the banquet and went into the garden; Haman then fell down before the queen to entreat for his life. When the king returned to the house, he saw Haman lying on the couch on which Esther was sitting, and thinking that he was offering violence to the queen, he passed sentence of death upon him, and caused him to be hanged on the tree he had erected for Mordochai (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.7-Esth.7.10">Est 7:7-10</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.6"/> <div eID="gen6774" type="x-p"/>

Then said the kings servants that ministred unto him, There is nothing done for him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He hath had no recompence for this great and good service<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Which might happen either through the Kings forgetfulness; or through the envy of the Courtiers; or because he was a Jew, and therefore odious and contemptible.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And the king said, Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the court? (now Haman was come <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Early in the morning, because his malice probably would not suffer him to sleep; and he was impatient till he had executed his desired revenge; an<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> he was resolved to watch for the very first opportunity of speaking to the King, before he was <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>gaged in o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther matters.</ns0:note> into the outward court of the kings house <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Where he wa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ed; because it was dangerous to come into the inuer Court without special licen<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4. 11.</ns0:note>, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the kings servants said unto him Behold, Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 So Haman came in, and the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He names none, because he would have the more impartial answer. And probably he knew nothing of the difference be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween <ns0:hi>Haman</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mordecai.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> honour the king delighteth.</ns0:note> whom the king delighteth to honour? (now Haman thought in his heart <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As indeed he had great reason to presume, because he had not yet for<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ed that favour which the King had shewed to him above all others.</ns0:note>, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to my self?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Haman answered the king, For the man <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> honour the king <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> whom the king delighteth to honour,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> them bring the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>l apparel.</ns0:note> Let the royal apparel <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">His outward garment which was made of purple, interwo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven with gold, as <ns0:hi>Iustin</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Curtius</ns0:hi> relate.</ns0:note> be brought, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with the king clotheth</ns0:hi> him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self.</ns0:note> which the king useth to wear, and the horse that the king rideth upon <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Usually: which was well known both by his excellency, and especially by his peculiar trappings and ornaments. Comp. 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 1. 33.</ns0:note>, and the crown royal which is set upon his head <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either 1. Up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the Kings head. Or, 2. Upon the Horses head<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which seems best to agree. 1. With that antient Chaldee Interpreter, and other Jews who take it thus. 2. With the signification and order of the Hebrew words. 3. With the following verses, in which there is no further mention of this Crown, but only of the <ns0:hi>apparel,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>horse,</ns0:hi> to which the Crown belonged as one of his ornaments. 4. With the custom of the <ns0:hi>Persians,</ns0:hi> which some affirm to have been this, to put the Crown upon the head of that Horse, upon which the King rode.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And let this apparel and horse be delivered to th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> hand of one of the kings most noble princes, that they may array the man <ns0:hi>withal,</ns0:hi> whom the king delighteth to honour, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> him to ride.</ns0:note> bring him on horseback through the principal street of the city, and proclaim <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Cause this to be proclaimed, to wit, by some publick Officer appointed for that service. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 41. 43.</ns0:note> before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lighteth to honour.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Then the king said to Haman, Make hast, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> take the apparel, and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the kings gate: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> not a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to fail.</ns0:note> let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then took Haman the apparel, and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either himself; or by the Officer.</ns0:note> before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:380" />12 And Mordecai came again to the kings gate <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To his former place and office; shewing that as he was not overwhelmed by <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> threats, and malicious design, as appears by <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 5. 9. So now he was not puf<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ed up with all this honour. Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sides, he came thither to attend the issue of the main business, and to be at hand to assist or encourage the Queen, if need were: which now he was more capable of doing than hitherto he had been.</ns0:note>: but Haman hasted to his house, mourning and having his head covered <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In token of his shame and grief for his unexpected, and great disappointment of his hope and desire, and for the great honour done to his most despised and abhorred adversary, and this by his own hands, and with his own publick disgrace; and for such fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther inconveniences as this unlucky omen seemed to presage to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Haman told Zeresh his wife, and all his friends, every <ns0:hi>thing</ns0:hi> that had befallen him. Then said his wise men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Magicians, whom after the Persian manner he had called together consult with upon this great and strange emergency.</ns0:note>, and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />decai <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> of the seed of the Jews <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which they were told, and was generally supposed, but they were not infallibly sure of it.</ns0:note>, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This they concluded, either 1. By rules of policy; because <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> reputation and interest was hereby sinking, and <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi> (whom they understood to be a man of great wisdom and courage, and government of himself) was now got into the Kings favour, and thereby was likely to gain an opportunity of making his addresses to the King, who being of a mild disposition, might easily be moved to a dislike (if not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vocation) of his own bloody decree, and consequently to a de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />testation of that person who had procured it. Or, 2. By former experience, and the observation of Gods extraordinary actions on the behalf of the Jews, and against their enemies in this very Court and Kingdom. Or, 3. By instinct and inspiration to their minds, either from God, who might suggest this to them, as he did other things to other wicked men, <ns0:hi>Balaam, Ca<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>aphas,</ns0:hi> &c. for his own greater glory, and the good of his people: or from the Devil; who by Gods permission, might know this, and reveal it to them who sought to him in their superstitious and idolatrous methods.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And while they <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> yet talking with him, came the kings chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Who was now slack to go thither, by reason of the great de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jection of his own mind, and the fear of a worse entertainment from the King and Queen than he had formerly received.</ns0:note> unto the banquet that Esther had prepared.</ns0:p>
